prompt: Before any training, the network fed raw pixels from 0 to 16 scores a loss of 15.42, against 2.45 for pixels from 0 to 1. Why?
hint: Look at the first layer's sums in the same table.

choices.text: The labels are stored on a different scale from the pixels
choices.why: The labels are the same digits 0 to 9 in all three versions; only the pixels changed.

choices.text: Its sums are spread 16 times wider, so the logits are large and confidently wrong
choices.why: Right: a standard deviation of 11.09 instead of 0.69. Large logits make softmax confident, and an untrained network confident is confident about the wrong class.

choices.text: Softmax works badly on inputs that are whole numbers
choices.why: The pixels are float32 in every version, and softmax sees logits, not pixels.

choices.text: The loss adds one term per pixel, and larger pixels add more
choices.why: Cross-entropy has one term per image, minus the log of the right class's probability; pixels never enter it directly.

prompt: At rate 0.01 the raw pixels reach 0.947 and the pixels from 0 to 1 only 0.897. What explains it?
hint: What does the scale of the inputs do to the size of a step?

choices.text: Raw ink levels carry fine detail that dividing every pixel by 16 removes
choices.why: Dividing by 16 loses nothing: every pixel keeps its order and its ratio to the others.

choices.text: The raw run overfits less, as lesson 7 would predict
choices.why: Overfitting is not what separates them; the same raw run collapses to chance at 0.3.

choices.text: Larger inputs take larger steps, so a small rate goes further
choices.why: Right. The scale works as part of the learning rate, which is also why the raw run breaks at 0.3 where the other does not.

choices.text: Dividing by 16 rounds small pixels to zero in float32
choices.why: float32 holds 1/16 exactly, and every level from 0 to 16 survives the division.

prompt: A network on a table with monthly income in reais and age in years trains badly at every rate tried. What is the first thing to change?
hint: Two features, two units, one learning rate.

choices.text: Standardise each column with the training set's mean and deviation
choices.why: Right. Income in thousands beside age in tens leaves no rate that suits both; after standardising, both columns are on the same footing.

choices.text: Standardise each column with the mean and deviation of all the rows, test included
choices.why: The idea is right and the statistics are not: computing them with the test rows leaks the test set into training.

choices.text: Keep lowering the rate until the loss falls
choices.why: A rate small enough for income is far too small for age, so one column learns and the other barely moves.

choices.text: Add hidden layers so the network has room to rescale the inputs
choices.why: Depth does not fix the first layer's steps, and this lesson shows deeper stacks are harder to keep stable.

prompt: Put what `BatchNorm.forward` does in training mode in order.
hint: The running averages are updated from what was just measured.
items: Measure each feature's mean and variance over the batch
Move the running averages 10% of the way towards them
Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation
Multiply by gamma and add beta

prompt: Why does batch norm multiply by `gamma` and add `beta` after normalising, when they could undo the normalisation?
hint: What would a ReLU do to a column fixed at mean 0?

choices.text: They hold the running statistics used in evaluation
choices.why: Those are `running_mean` and `running_var`, which no gradient moves; `gamma` and `beta` are trained.

choices.text: So each unit learns its own mean and spread, as a parameter
choices.why: Right. Fixed at mean 0, a ReLU after it would cut about half of every column; now the spread is learnt rather than an accident of the weights.

choices.text: They stand in for the learning rate inside the layer
choices.why: The optimiser's rate still sets every step, theirs included.

choices.text: Without them the backward pass would have no gradient to send back to the layer
choices.why: The input gradient exists without them; with `gamma` at 1 it is the same formula with `g = grad`.

prompt: How many trained parameters does `BatchNorm(64)` have?
hint: Count only what `params` names; the running averages are not trained.

prompt: In a block of `Linear`, then `BatchNorm`, then `ReLU`, what does the `Linear` layer's bias contribute to the block's output in training?
hint: Add a constant to a column, then subtract the column's mean.

choices.text: It moves the point where the ReLU starts to pass values
choices.why: That is `beta`'s job here; the bias is gone before the ReLU sees anything.

choices.text: It doubles the shift `beta` applies
choices.why: The bias is added before the mean is subtracted, so it cannot reach the output to add to `beta`.

choices.text: Nothing: subtracting the batch mean removes it
choices.why: Right. A constant added to every row of a column shifts its mean by the same amount, and the subtraction takes both away.

choices.text: It keeps evaluation mode working when the running mean is zero
choices.why: Evaluation subtracts the running mean, which learnt the bias in along with everything else; the result is the same.

prompt: Without normalisation at rate 0.1, the ten-layer network reaches 0.867 at epoch 10 and falls to 0.356 at epoch 15. What does that shape say?
hint: Lesson 6 read curves by their shape.

choices.text: The network overfit the training set
choices.why: Overfitting lets validation drift down slowly while training improves; a drop of half the accuracy in five epochs is a step too large.

choices.text: The rate is too high for it
choices.why: Right. The same rate with batch norm climbs to 0.972, so it is the network without normalisation that cannot take it.

choices.text: The starting weights were unlucky for this seed
choices.why: Both runs start from the same weights, and the one with batch norm trains.

choices.text: The data ran out, so the network kept seeing batches it had already seen
choices.why: Every epoch reuses the whole training set by design; repeating it is what epochs are.

prompt: A large step triples every weight of one unit in the `Linear` layer just before a batch norm layer. What happens to that unit's `xhat`?
hint: Sums, mean and standard deviation all scale together.

choices.text: It triples, and so does everything after it
choices.why: That is what happens without normalisation, and it is the effect that multiplies through ten layers.

choices.text: Its variance grows ninefold
choices.why: The sums' variance does, and the layer divides by its square root, three, again.

choices.text: It does not change
choices.why: Right. The sums, their mean and their deviation all triple, and the ratio stays put, which is why the layers after it see the same scale.

choices.text: It shrinks to a third
choices.why: Dividing by a deviation three times larger is cancelled by sums three times larger.

prompt: Batch norm does not make a good rate much better; what it does is make a large rate ___.
hint: Compare the two tables at 0.03 and at 0.3.

prompt: In training mode, every image predicted on its own got the same logits. Why?
hint: What are the mean and variance of a batch of one?

choices.text: The running averages had not yet been filled in by enough training batches
choices.why: Training mode does not read the running averages; it measures the batch in front of it.

choices.text: A batch of one has variance 0, so `xhat` is 0 and the layer outputs `beta`
choices.why: Right. With a variance of 0, every feature normalises to 0, and `beta` is the same vector for every image.

choices.text: `gamma` learnt to be zero during training
choices.why: In evaluation mode the same `gamma` gives five right answers, so it is not zero.

choices.text: Softmax saturates when the batch holds a single image
choices.why: Softmax works row by row and does not know the batch size; the logits were equal before it.

prompt: After five single images went through in training mode, validation loss rose from 0.138 to 0.166 although nobody trained the network. What changed?
hint: Training mode does two things in `forward`.

choices.text: The weights moved, because `forward` in training mode also takes a step
choices.why: A step needs `backward` and `opt.step()`; `forward` alone never touches `W`, `gamma` or `beta`.

choices.text: `evaluate` reused logits cached from the training-mode calls
choices.why: `evaluate` runs a fresh forward pass over the whole validation set.

choices.text: `gamma` shrank towards zero
choices.why: `gamma` is a parameter and only the optimiser moves it.

choices.text: The running variance, which each call moved 10% towards zero
choices.why: Right: from 0.1114 to 0.0658 for the first feature. Evaluation then divides by a deviation that is too small.

prompt: A served model gives one image a different class depending on which other requests are batched with it. What is the most likely cause?
hint: Which mode lets one row's output depend on the others?

choices.text: Floating-point rounding differs from batch to batch
choices.why: Rounding moves the last digits of a logit, not the class; the effect here is the batch statistics.

choices.text: The model is running in training mode, normalising with each batch's statistics
choices.why: Right. In evaluation mode every row uses the running averages, and an image's answer does not depend on its company.

choices.text: The weights were saved before training finished
choices.why: Weights saved early give worse answers, but the same answer whatever the batch.

choices.text: The learning rate was too high for the batch size used in production
choices.why: Serving takes no steps, so the rate plays no part.

prompt: Match each layer, in each situation, to what it does.

pairs.right: the same output it gives inside a batch
divides by the root mean square, without subtracting the mean

right_distractors: normalises with the statistics of the next batch

prompt: Why do transformers use layer norm rather than batch norm?
hint: Think about padded sentences and writing one token at a time.

choices.text: Layer norm has no parameters to train
choices.why: It has the same `gamma` and `beta`, one per feature.

choices.text: It needs only each token's own features
choices.why: Right. Batch statistics would mix words with padding, and generation runs one token at a time for one user.

choices.text: Batch norm has no backward pass through attention
choices.why: Its backward is the formula this lesson checked, and it works after any layer.

choices.text: Layer norm stabilises every kind of network more than batch norm does
choices.why: Not on this lesson's ten-layer network: at rate 1.0 it failed where batch norm reached 0.961.

prompt: A colleague sees layer norm fail at rate 1.0 on the digits network and concludes it is useless. What is wrong with the conclusion?

choices.text: It is meant for where batch statistics make no sense, not for images
choices.why: Right. On fully connected layers over images batch norm is stronger; layer norm is the one that keeps working on a batch of one.

choices.text: Nothing: a layer that fails at one rate has no use
choices.why: At 0.1 and 0.3 it trained a network that failed without it.

choices.text: Layer norm needs a much larger `eps` before it can train at high rates
choices.why: `eps` only guards against dividing by zero; nothing in the run points at it.

choices.text: The run was in training mode, and layer norm only works in evaluation mode
choices.why: Layer norm has no mode; it computes the same thing in training and in use.

prompt: Which of these did this lesson's runs show? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Raw pixels from 0 to 16 fell to chance at rate 0.3
choices.why: Yes: 0.089, against 0.969 for the scaled pixels.

choices.text: With batch norm, the ten-layer network trained at rate 1.0
choices.why: Yes: it ended at 0.961, where the network without it had a `nan` loss.

choices.text: Batch norm beat no normalisation by a wide margin at rate 0.03
choices.why: No: 0.969 against 0.961 at the end; the large gains were at the higher rates.

choices.text: Layer norm gave an image the same output alone as in a batch
choices.why: Yes: the same six numbers both times.

choices.text: Predicting in training mode changed the network's weights
choices.why: No: it changed the running variance, which is not a weight; no step was taken.

prompt: With `momentum=0.1`, a batch of variance 0 multiplies the running variance by what factor?
hint: `(1 - m) * running + m * var`, with `var` at 0.

prompt: A network with batch norm trained with batches of 2 images gives erratic results. Why?
hint: How good is a mean measured from two examples?

choices.text: Batch norm needs at least as many examples in each batch as it has features
choices.why: No such rule exists; it needs two rows for a variance, and more for a steady one.

choices.text: Two images give noisy statistics, so each output hinges on its partner
choices.why: Right. With two rows, every normalised value is close to +1 or -1, which says only which of the pair is larger.

choices.text: The momentum of 0.1 is too high for batches that small
choices.why: Momentum affects only the running averages for evaluation; the erratic part is training itself.

choices.text: `gamma` and `beta` receive no gradient at all from batches of only two
choices.why: Their gradients are sums over the batch and exist for any size.
